opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a really evocative phrase. The way I understand it, Spelke's broader picture is that infants come equipped with a handful of core knowledge systems: objects, agents, number, places, geometry, and so on. Each of these is fairly encapsulated and domain-specific. What's distinctive about humans, on her account, is that language, or more generally a compositional system of representation, lets us take the primitives from these separate systems and glue them together in new ways. You can think "the red thing to the left of the tall agent," crossing color, geometry and agency in one thought. That's the blessing: an unbounded space of thoughts built from a finite base.

The curse is the flip side of exactly that power. Once you can compose anything with anything, the space of possible thoughts, hypotheses, or explanations becomes astronomically large. Most of those compositions are irrelevant, false, or just nonsense. So a compositional mind constantly faces the problem of which combinations to actually entertain. Expressiveness buys you generality, but it costs you search, and it costs you the ability to be wrong in many more ways than a narrow, specialized system can be.

That resonates a lot with my own work in program synthesis. A programming language is the canonical compositional system. If your DSL is rich enough, the program that explains your data is in there somewhere, but you're now searching an exponentially growing space, and many programs fit the data equally well. So you need something more: good inductive biases, priors over which compositions are likely, and learned abstractions that compress useful patterns so the search gets shallower. In DreamCoder, a lot of the point was that a library learned from experience changes which programs are short, and therefore which thoughts are easy to have.

So I read Spelke's curse less as a reason to abandon compositionality and more as a statement of the central problem any compositional learner has to solve. You get to say anything, so now you need to know what's worth saying. Humans handle that with some mix of core knowledge constraining the primitives, accumulated abstractions, and intuitions about what's plausible, which I'd now increasingly think of as learned, neural-style guidance over a symbolic space. Getting that balance right, a compositional representation plus good learned intuitions about how to navigate it, is to me one of the most interesting open questions in building machines that learn like people.

r001.rationale: The response says compositionality creates an “astronomically large” space of possible thoughts, hypotheses, and explanations, and describes the search space as growing exponentially.

r002.rationale: It explains that being able to compose anything does not identify which combinations are worth considering, and says learners need priors, inductive biases, and plausibility guidance.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it, Spelke's point is that compositionality is what makes human cognition so powerful, but it's also what makes it slow and effortful. If you have a mind that can combine pieces into new structures, you've bought yourself enormous flexibility, and the price you pay is that you now have to search. You have to figure out which pieces to combine and how. A system that just pattern-matches doesn't have that problem, because it's not building anything. It just retrieves.

And you see this really clearly in kids. Spelke's work on core knowledge shows that infants come in with these little systems, for objects, for agents, for number, for geometry, and each one on its own is fast and automatic. The hard part, the thing that takes years and that language seems to be deeply involved in, is gluing them together. Taking "left of the blue wall" and actually composing the geometry with the color. Kids can do each half early, but combining them is late and fragile. So the curse is that having a compositional mind doesn't mean composition is free. It means you've inherited a combinatorial search problem.

From my side, in program synthesis, that's exactly the thing we fight with every day. The moment you say "my hypothesis space is programs," you've got this beautiful, expressive, generalizable representation, and you've also got a space that explodes. Most of the engineering in something like DreamCoder is about taming that: learning a library so that the useful compositions become single primitives, and learning a neural recognition model so you don't have to search blindly. I actually think that's a pretty reasonable story for what the brain is doing too. You amortize. The things you've composed many times get cached and become fast, and then the curse only bites on the genuinely novel stuff.

So I don't read it as pessimistic. I read it as an explanation of why thinking is hard and why learning is slow, and also as a hint that the right architecture isn't "composition or pattern-matching," it's both, where the pattern-matching part exists precisely to pay down the cost of the compositional part.

r001.rationale: The response says composition creates a combinatorial search problem and that a program hypothesis space “explodes,” clearly describing the growth of possible compositions.

r002.rationale: It says a compositional mind must search for which pieces to combine, but does not clearly state that representational capacity alone fails to guide the mind toward concepts plausible in the current context.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that compositionality gives us this extraordinary ability to take concepts we already have and combine them into new thoughts. But the same ability creates a problem: there are vastly more thoughts you could construct than thoughts that are useful or worth considering. So being able to represent something doesn’t tell you how to find it.

In program synthesis, you see this very clearly. You have a small set of primitives and ways of combining them, and suddenly you can express an enormous range of programs. But now you have to search that space. Most of those programs won’t solve your problem, and even many that do won’t capture the explanation you were looking for.

So I take the curse to be the other side of that expressive power. What makes human thinking interesting isn’t just that we can compose things; it’s that we’re often able to find the right compositions without exhaustively trying all the possibilities. That’s where learning, experience, and the structure of our prior knowledge have to come in.

r001.rationale: It says compositionality lets us combine concepts into vastly more possible thoughts and express an enormous range of programs, describing a combinatorial expansion of representations.

r002.rationale: It says representational ability alone does not tell us how to find useful thoughts or the right compositions, and identifies learning, experience, and prior knowledge as needed guidance.

sol-6.1.text:
My understanding is that compositionality gives us this extraordinary ability to take a few concepts and combine them into thoughts we’ve never had before. But that creates a problem: the space of things you can think becomes much larger than the space of things that make sense or are useful.

So if I give you a handful of objects and relations, you can construct endlessly many descriptions or explanations. The fact that you can compose them doesn’t tell you which ones are worth considering. That’s the curse: the same machinery that makes thought productive also creates a huge search problem.

From a program synthesis perspective, that feels very familiar. A small set of primitives can express an enormous number of programs. Expressivity is wonderful, but you still need something that guides you toward the tiny fraction of programs that actually explain the data. So the question becomes how learning and prior knowledge make that compositional space manageable.

r001.rationale: The response says compositionality lets a few concepts generate endlessly many descriptions and creates a huge search space, conveying a combinatorial explosion in possible representations.

r002.rationale: It explains that the ability to compose ideas does not identify which are useful, and that guidance is needed to find the small fraction that explain the data.
